title: Require accuracy testing and human review before facial recognition triggers any adverse action against a customer
description: Illustrative reference decision modelled on the FTC's enforcement action against Rite Aid. Not a documented decision of any specific organisation.

history.note: Initial Phase 2A seed content, part of the Foundational Twenty.

decision_statement: Facial recognition used for loss-prevention or surveillance purposes must be tested for accuracy and false-match rate across demographic groups before deployment, and a facial-recognition match alone must never trigger an adverse action against a customer (denial of service, accusation, removal) without a trained human independently confirming the match first.
decision_context: Motivated by the FTC's finding that Rite Aid deployed facial recognition without reasonable safeguards, causing employees to act on false-positive alerts that disproportionately harmed Black, Asian, Latino, and women consumers.
governing_body: Illustrative example — Biometric Systems Governance Board
alternatives_considered: Permit staff to act immediately on any facial-recognition alert without independent confirmation.
Rely on the vendor's claimed accuracy figures without independent, demographic-disaggregated testing.

citations.title: Rite Aid Banned from Using AI Facial Recognition After FTC Says Retailer Deployed Technology without Reasonable Safeguards

relationships.reason: This decision is modelled as a direct governance response to this enforcement action.
The decision is put into practice via this design pattern.
Accuracy testing and a human-confirmation step address the unfairness theory the FTC applied under this authority.
Compliance must be demonstrated by a documented accuracy and human-review log.
Boards adopting this decision should be asking whether biometric systems have documented consent and accuracy safeguards.
